nodes.question: Why must GI be specifically designed and tailored according to the paragraph?
nodes.answer: GI must be specifically designed and tailored to consider specific local conditions and needs.
nodes.paragraph: This means that GI must be specifically designed and tailored while considering specific local condi- tions and needs (Mantilla et al., 2023). As a result, the same GI (e.g., green roofs, green walls) implemented in different locations within a geographical catchment may have a broad range of differing performance and cost-effective features (Webber & Kuller, 2021). Literature also show that intensive green roofs perform better than extensive green roofs in thermal insulation, stormwater management and the provision of recrea- tion (Aleksejeva et al., 2024). The current study by Cook et al. (2024) sheds light on the multifunctionality concept in GI projects, clearly depicting that GI design requires intentional considerations, thereby refuting the passive design notion. From the forgo- ing, it is clear that knowledge of the multifunctionality concept is crucial to ensure that GI achieve the intended objectives and functionality. Given that built environment pro- fessionals provide technical knowledge and expertise towards the execution of GI pro- jects, it is expedient to investigate the knowledge levels of GI from the perspective of these technical experts to provide relevant knowledge toward effective communication, design, implementation and monitoring.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Localized climate change action plans_qna_004
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What method did the researchers use to analyze the climate action plans of U.S. cities?
nodes.answer: The researchers conducted a qualitative content analysis of CAPs published by U.S. cities between 2018 and early 2023.
nodes.paragraph: In this research, we ask to what extent city CAPs can contribute to meaningful climate action at the local level. Through a review of CAPs published by U.S. cities between 2018 and early 2023, we conducted a qualitative content analysis of these documents to better understand the current state of climate action planning, to ask how U.S. cities are approaching climate action, and to make recommenda - tions to strengthen both research and practice. 1.1 Background on climate action planning As an initial step in the climate action planning process, cities measure and report their GHG emissions through a GHG inventory. Urban regions are key sources of emissions, accounting for over 70% of total GHG emissions (Ruth et al. 2017 ; United Nations 2019 ). Three sectors accounted for 77% of total GHG emissions in the United States: Transporta - tion (28%), Electric Power (25%), and Industry (23%) (U.S. EPA 2024). Conversely, munic - ipally owned facilities only account for 5% of a community S total emissions. (City of Raleigh 2016 ).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Localized climate change action plans_qna_005
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What proportion of climate action strategies is focused on creating new plans and assessments?
nodes.answer: Nearly half, specifically 49%, of all strategies focus on creating new plans and assessments.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Cities are increasingly creating climate action plans (CAPs), but it is unclear what poten - tial these have for cities to sufficiently address the climate crisis. We conducted a review of 157 CAPs published by U.S. cities between 2018 and early 2023 to assess the current state of the practice. Through a qualitative content analysis of these plans, we analyzed explicit planned strategies to describe what sectors receive the most attention, what types of actions cities commonly take, and what domains of urban life are most leveraged to solving climate change. We found that a strong plurality (40%) of all strategies target municipal operations, nearly half (49%) of all strategies are focused on creating new plans and assessments, and energy and mobility contribute to nearly half (43%) of all strategies. These findings identify shortcomings of conventional climate action planning, including opportunity to work across sectors, to create stronger interventions, and to integrate cli - mate action across all urban domains, including food and water. Climate action planning has become a ubiquitous practice for cities, and cities climate action will continue to in - crease in importance over the next decade.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Localized climate change action plans_qna_009
nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What are climate action plans (CAPs)?
nodes.answer: Climate action plans (CAPs) are documents wherein cities detail a comprehensive understanding of climate change, inventory and report their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and set goals and objectives for action, leading to tangible policy outcomes.
nodes.paragraph: While cities have been pursuing climate action for over twenty years, we are still observing early stages of its evolution. This research identifies areas to improve climate action planning and concludes with recommendations for practice. Keywords Climate action SDG 13 Scoping review SDG 11 Climate planning 1 Introduction As the world rapidly urbanizes during the climate crisis, cities face the challenge of act - ing on climate change. Though climate change is a global concern, its drivers and impacts stem from and shape human activity at a local scale. With a projected 68% of the world S population residing in urban areas by 2050, cities may be well-positioned to monitor their 1 3 Climatic Change (2025) 178:61 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and implement strategies centered around mitigation and adaptation (Dams et al. 2016 ; United Nations 2019 ). To organize and communicate their goals on climate, cities typically draft climate action plans (CAPs). CAPs are documents wherein cities detail a comprehensive understanding of climate change, inventory and report their GHG emissions, and set goals and objectives for action, leading hopefully to tangible policy outcomes.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Localized climate change action plans_qna_011
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What challenges do many cities face regarding climate action plans (CAPs)?
nodes.answer: Many cities struggle to integrate both mitigation and adaptation strategies into their climate action plans (CAPs).
nodes.paragraph: While past research has documented a disproportionate emphasis on mitigation strategies in American cities (Ozcan and Strauss 2021 ), adaptation is growing in importance (Tang et al. 2010 ; Shi et al. 2015 ; Grafakos et al. 2019 ), though research has shown that many cit - ies struggle to integrate mitigation and adaptation into their CAPs (Aboagye and Sharifi 2024 ). Adaptation can occur at state and national levels; however, adaptation is inherently a local issue, where climate change renders cities vulnerable to impacts such as flooding and drought, among other challenges (Corfee-Morlot et al. 2010 ; Bierbaum et al. 2012 ; Hughes 2015 ; Greve 2016 ). Adaptation strategies may also appear in other planning documents, including resilience plans, which have increased in popularity in recent years (Lambrou and Loukaitou-Sideris 2021 ). 1.2 Local powers and local climate policy We noted above U.S. cities tendencies to target mitigation strategies on emissions from municipal facilities and other domains that are easily managed by their jurisdictional pow - ers. For this research, we study a dataset of CAPs published over a recent five-year period, asking in part whether this trend has changed or if municipal operations still dominate cli - mate action planning in the U.S.
